title: All flame (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)
hookLine: an old monk raises his hands and says why not become all flame
tomorrow: what does a saint do when the walls fill up with roaring?

cards: Every box is checked. The application is in, the follow-up email is sent, the extra practice is done, and the answer still hasn't come. So what else is there?

A desert monk named Lot asked exactly that. He'd kept his short daily prayers, his little fasting, his quiet, his peace. He walked over to an older monk, Abba Joseph, and asked: what more should I do?
The old man answered without a list.

teach.b: This is from the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, short stories and words of monks and nuns who lived in the Egyptian desert, handed on one saying at a time. First, the modest rule.

Lot's list is good, and Joseph doesn't criticize a single item on it. A little prayer, a little fasting, quiet, peace, a heart he keeps clearing of bad thoughts as far as he can. Second, the question.
As far as I can, Lot says, I do these things.
What else? He isn't bragging. He's asking whether there's more to this than doing things well.
Joseph stands up and stretches his hands toward heaven, and the story says his fingers became like lamps of fire. Fourth, the answer.
If you will, he says, you can become all flame. He doesn't add a practice to the list.

He points past it, to a life set alight all the way through. On a week when the list is done and nothing has moved, the saying turns the question around. Not what else can I do, but what could all of this be burning for?
The saying never explains itself, and that seems to be the point: Lot came for one more task and went home with a picture.

how: Catholics read the Sayings of the Desert Fathers in monasteries and in private prayer; at Mass the priest prays with hands extended, an old gesture of prayer.

o: a life set alight, beyond the checklist
a monk's punishment for breaking his rule
a fast with no food until the sun goes down

p: the monk with the finished checklist
the old monk who raised his hands
what Lot could become, if he willed

s: Abba Joseph told Lot his rule was too small
he criticized nothing on the list. he pointed past it.
the story says Joseph's fingers became like lamps of fire
he stood, stretched his hands toward heaven, and then answered.
the desert sayings were long sermons written for crowds
they're short stories and words, handed on one at a time.

games.q: your coworker volunteers at a food bank, goes to every parish event, and still feels flat inside. she asks what she's missing. which answer is closest to Abba Joseph's?
o: not another task: let what you already do catch fire.
you're doing too little, so sign up for one more thing.
quit everything until the good feeling comes back.
games.why: Joseph honored Lot's whole list and added nothing to it. he raised his hands, his fingers like lamps of fire, and said: if you will, you can become all flame.

practice: Stand if you can, or sit tall, and raise your hands, palms open, the way Abba Joseph did. Stay there for a few slow breaths, and lower your arms whenever they need a rest. Let the open hands hold your own question: what else?

wordCard.voice: All flame. The desert's answer to what comes after the checklist: not one more task, but a whole life alight.

orig.note: Greek for fire: the old monk's fingers became like lamps of it.

carryVoice: Carry this: all flame, because the list was good and the fire was more. On we go.
